<reason>B made the stronger incremental case for allowing pricing alongside enforcement: anticipated charges can influence consolidation, dispatch, and stopping duration even when particular trips cannot shift. A raised genuine concerns about fee incidence and decision-making control, but repeatedly treated concessions about inflexible trips as proof that meaningful flexibility never exists. B also successfully defended demand-responsive prices with locked commitments and showed why queues impose unequal costs too. A’s sharp rhetoric did not establish that large fleets would ignore charges while smaller operators necessarily exit.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B’s response to the florist example exposed the weakness in calling waiting equally affordable: equal minutes do not mean equal burdens when one operator has only one van. Combined with the point that recurring charges can influence even wealthy fleets, this substantially weakened A’s central fairness comparison.</best_rebuttal>
